newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges schools to require volunteerism.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges schools to require volunteerism.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, preparing for a national service summit later this month, on Saturday urged schools and communities to make volunteer service a part of the curriculum for students.

"Every young American should be taught the joy and the duty of serving, and should learn it at the moment when it will have the most enduring impact on the rest of their lives," Clinton said in his weekly radio address.
Clinton was stressing the need for more citizens to volunteer their time and talents to help people ahead of The Presidents' Summit for America's Future, scheduled for April 27-29 in Philadelphia.

Clinton, along with former President George Bush and retired Gen. Colin Powell, are to attend the summit which will bring together community representatives from around the country to discuss how to increase help for the needy, especially children.
Former President Gerald Ford and former first ladies Lady Bird Johnson and Nancy Reagan are expected to participate as well in what Clinton has called an unprecedented national summons to service.
In his radio address, Clinton said states should follow the lead of Maryland, the first state to require that every student perform some service as a condition of high school graduation.

He cited examples of service from among the Maryland students who watched him deliver his radio address: some gather food and clothing for the needy, some teach disabled students, others tutor young children.
"Today I challenge schools and communities in every state to make service a part of the curriculum in high school and even in middle school," he said.

He said that as a means to promote the idea, students could be given credit for the tasks, service could be made part of the curriculum, service could be put on a student's transcript or it could even be required, like Maryland.
He pointed to a recent Brandeis University study that found well-designed service learning programmes can improve learning, strengthen civic attitudes and promote service activities.

It was the type of small-scale initiative that Clinton pushed during his 1996 re-election campaign, during which he promoted ideas like requiring school uniforms for students. His national service programme, AmeriCorps, emerged from his 1992 campaign.
Lest anyone think he was proposing a new mandate for states, Clinton added: "States and schools, of course, should be free to decide this for themselves."

Clinton announced the start of his National Service Scholars programme, in which high schools can recognise young people for outstanding service by awarding them $1,000 scholarships. The U.S. government will pay half and civic organisations like the Lions Club and the Jaycees are working to provide the rest.

In answer to Clinton's appeal, the White House said the National Association of Secondary School Principals, representing more than 40,000 school administrators, has pledged to introduce service learning to more than 2 million students.
